statement: In 142 healthy adults with little drug experience and no psychiatric history who took LSD and/or psilocybin in six placebo-controlled laboratory trials in Switzerland (Müller et al., 2022), 13 (9.2%) described flashback-like experiences when asked at the end of the study: 7 of 90 after LSD only, 2 of 24 after psilocybin only and 4 of 28 after both. They were mostly single, brief visual changes lasting seconds to minutes, mostly in the days right after the last session, and 10 of the 13 felt neutral or pleasant; 2 people (1.4%) found them distressing, one of whom went on to have panic attacks and left the study, and one person had brief visual flashbacks, which she felt as positive, on and off for seven months. No one reported problems in daily life and no one was found to meet the criteria for hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD); with no case among 142 people, a true rate of up to about 2% cannot be ruled out (editors' calculation). There was no comparison with how often similar experiences happen without a drug, and the participants were screened volunteers, so rates in recreational use may differ. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: About 1 in 11 healthy volunteers who took LSD or psilocybin in lab studies said they later had a flashback, usually a short change in what they saw, in the days after. Most did not mind it; 2 of 142 were upset by it. Nobody developed lasting vision problems. These were careful lab studies with screened people, so it may be different in everyday use.
population: Healthy adults aged 25 to 65 with little previous drug use and no personal or family psychiatric history, in six placebo-controlled crossover trials in Basel (142 people, 74 women)
exposure: LSD and/or psilocybin given in the trials
comparator: None for the flashback outcome (frequencies are descriptive)
outcome: Flashback phenomena reported at the end-of-study visit and at follow-up; DSM-5 hallucinogen persisting perception disorder
magnitude: 13 of 142 (9.2%): LSD only 7 of 90 (7.8%), psilocybin only 2 of 24 (8.3%), both 4 of 28 (14.3%); distressing 2 of 142 (1.4%); HPPD 0 of 142 (editors' calculation: one-sided 95% upper limit about 2.1%). Mostly visual (11 of 13), seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%); single occurrence in 53.8%.

evidence.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: 13 of 142 participants (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena at the end-of-study visit: 7 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 after psilocybin only (8.3%), 4 after both (14.3%). 11 were visual, 2 purely emotional; most lasted seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%), one hours; 53.8% occurred once; in all but two cases they were limited to the week after the last drug administration; over half occurred while relaxing or around sleep.

evidence.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Flashbacks were unpleasant for 2 (1.4% of all 142) and neutral or positive for 10; one case was not sufficiently documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session and the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.

evidence.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Flashback phenomena at follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: One participant had about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later, 12 of 13 responding, one incompletely) she was the only one who clearly reported recurrence after the end-of-study visit.

No participant met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD; the simulated chance of seeing no case in 142 people was 24.0% at a true incidence of 1%, 5.7% at 2% and 1.3% at 3%. Editors' calculation: zero events in 142 gives a one-sided 95% upper limit of about 2.1%.

evidence.locator: Methods › Inclusion and exclusion criteria of studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Exclusions included current or previous psychotic or major psychiatric disorder, psychotic disorder in a first-degree relative, and more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted). Three of the 13 had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA. The authors list the sample size, varied doses and substances, likely positive attitudes, follow-up only of those with flashbacks, and exclusion of people with mental disorders as limitations.

risk_of_bias.note: One open question at intervals of 2 to 193 days, no standard instrument, follow-up only of those reporting flashbacks, no no-drug comparison: the figure could be materially higher or lower (JBI moderate on the card).

indirectness.note: Worded for screened volunteers in controlled trials.

imprecision.note: The HPPD upper limit is stated in the claim.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low (METHODS 6.3) and is rated down because the way flashbacks were asked about could change the figure materially; very low. Status single study: one pooled analysis of one group's six trials.
